title: Shape decides what molecules do
question: How does the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms affect a molecule?
hook: Two substances built from the same atoms can behave in very different ways.
idea: The three-dimensional arrangement of a molecule's atoms influences its reactivity, polarity, phase of matter, color, magnetism and biological activity.

beats.prompt: Two compounds have the same chemical formula, but their atoms are not bonded together in the same order. What do you expect?

choices.label: Identical properties, since the formula is the same
choices.feedback: The formula lists the atoms, which tempts people to expect the same behaviour, but the arrangement matters.

choices.label: Often different geometries and very different properties
The same molecule drawn in two ways
choices.feedback: A different bonding order makes a different molecule, not a different drawing.

beats.explain: Structural isomers share a formula but bond their atoms in a different order, often giving alternate geometries with very different properties.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it describes.
pairs: Average distance between two bonded nuclei
Angle formed between three atoms across at least two bonds
Angle between the planes of the first and last three atoms in a four-atom chain
Atomic orbitals of bonding atoms combining
beats.explain: Geometry is specified by lengths and angles, and bonding itself involves orbitals combining.

beats.prompt: Sort each type of isomer by how its atoms are connected.
groups: Atoms bonded in a different order
items: Atoms bonded in a different order
Atoms bonded in a different order
beats.explain: Structural (constitutional) isomers change the connection order; stereoisomers, which divide into enantiomers and diastereomers, keep it and change the orientation in space.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about measuring geometry is wrong. Which?
steps: Many spectroscopic results are averaged over rotational states.
A higher temperature means more rotational states are populated and averaged.
More averaging makes the geometry easier to extract from the spectrum.
So reliable geometries are best expected at temperatures close to absolute zero.
beats.explain: More averaging makes geometries harder to extract, which is why reliable results come from temperatures close to absolute zero.
